topics.title: A reference is another name for one object
topics.body: A reference must bind at initialization and never rebinds, so writing through it always reaches the same object. That makes reference parameters a readable way to return results through the argument list.

topics.title: nullptr is a type, not a macro
topics.body: `nullptr` has type `std::nullptr_t` and converts to any pointer type without becoming an integer. `NULL` is usually `0`, which overloads can mistake for an int.

tasks.title: Sum an array through a pointer
tasks.statement: Walk `{2, 4, 6}` with a pointer from the first element to one past the last, and print the total.

debug.error: the program failed at runtime (exit null)

interview.q: What is the difference between a pointer and a reference?
interview.answer: A pointer is an object that stores an address and can be null or reassigned; a reference is an alias that must be bound and cannot be reseated. References have no null state, which removes one class of bug when the target is required.
The object it points at is destroyed or freed while the pointer still holds the old address. Reading or writing through it is undefined, so lifetime has to outlive every pointer to it.

mcq.q: Which statement is true of a reference?
options: It can be reseated after binding
It must be bound when initialized
mcq.answer: It must be bound when initialized
mcq.why: A reference is an alias and cannot be rebound or left unbound.
The dedicated type avoids the integer interpretation that `NULL` has.

topics.title: unique_ptr frees itself
topics.body: `std::make_unique` allocates and hands ownership to a `unique_ptr`, whose destructor calls `delete`. No manual cleanup remains on the success path or on a thrown exception.

topics.title: shared_ptr counts its owners
topics.body: A `shared_ptr` keeps a control block with a strong count; copying increments it and destruction decrements it, freeing the object at zero. `use_count` reports the current number of owners.

tasks.title: Own a dynamic array safely
tasks.statement: Allocate four ints with `make_unique<int[]>`, fill them with 1 to 4, sum them and print the total.

interview.q: What does RAII mean in practice?
interview.answer: A resource is acquired by an object’s constructor and released by its destructor, so scope and the type system guarantee cleanup. It works for memory, files, locks and sockets alike.

It allocates the object and the control block in one allocation, which is faster and exception-safe. The raw `new` form can leak if an exception occurs between allocation and the smart pointer construction.

mcq.q: What happens when a `unique_ptr` goes out of scope?
Which smart pointer allows several owners?
mcq.why: A shared pointer keeps a reference count across copies.

topics.title: enum class keeps its names inside the enum
topics.body: A scoped enum requires `Level::High` at every use and does not convert to int implicitly. That removes the collisions and accidental arithmetic that plain enums allow.

topics.title: Structured bindings unpack a tuple
topics.body: `auto [name, marks] = student;` declares one variable per element and binds them to the tuple’s members. It also works on pairs, arrays and simple structs.

tasks.title: Sum marks in a struct array
tasks.statement: Define a `Student` struct with a name and marks; create three students and print the total marks.

debug.title: A scoped enum used as an int
debug.error: error: cannot convert ‘Color’ to ‘int’ in initialization

interview.q: When is a plain enum still acceptable?
interview.answer: When the names are local to one small scope and implicit integer conversion is convenient, such as indexing a table. A scoped enum is the safer default because it prevents accidental mixing with integers.

interview.q: What is the difference between a struct and a class in C++?
interview.answer: Only the default access: struct members are public and class members are private, and inheritance defaults follow the same rule. Everything else, including constructors and methods, is identical.

mcq.q: How do you refer to the `High` enumerator of `enum class Level`?
mcq.why: Scoped enumerators are qualified by the enum name.

mcq.q: What does a structured binding declare?
mcq.why: Each name binds to the corresponding tuple, pair, array or struct member.

topics.title: A class enforces its invariant
topics.body: Keeping `balance` private and validating inside `deposit` means no caller can create a negative balance. The public methods are the only way to change the state, so the rule holds everywhere.

topics.title: const member functions promise not to mutate
topics.body: A `const` member function can be called on a const object and may not modify members. Marking the readers const is what lets the rest of the program pass objects by const reference.

tasks.title: A rectangle with area and perimeter
tasks.statement: Write a `Rectangle` class with width and height, and member functions `area()` and `perimeter()`; print both for 3 by 4.

debug.title: Members left private by default

interview.q: What is encapsulation, beyond private members?
interview.answer: It is the guarantee that state can only change through operations that preserve its rules. Private data is the mechanism; a validated interface is the point.

interview.q: What does `this` point to inside a member function?
interview.answer: The object the call was made on, with the member function’s constness applied. It is why `return *this;` enables chaining and why a const member function has a pointer to const.

mcq.q: What is the default access for members of a `class`?
mcq.why: Unlike a struct, a class starts private.

mcq.q: What does a const member function guarantee?
options: It cannot modify the object’s members
mcq.answer: It cannot modify the object’s members
mcq.why: The const qualifier forbids mutation except for mutable members.

topics.title: Initialization lists run before the body
topics.body: Members are constructed in declaration order before the constructor body executes, so an initializer list is the only place to construct a const or reference member. Listing them in a different order than declared invites confusion.

topics.title: A delegating constructor reuses another
topics.body: `Box() : Box(0) {}` hands construction to the parameterized constructor, so the default state is defined in exactly one place. This keeps validation from being duplicated.

tasks.title: Construct with defaults and arguments
tasks.statement: Write a `Student` class whose default constructor sets marks to 0 and whose parameterized constructor takes marks; print both objects.

debug.title: A constructor with the wrong name
debug.error: error: ISO C++ forbids declaration of ‘account’ with no type [-fpermissive]

interview.q: What is the Rule of Three?
interview.answer: If a class needs a custom destructor, copy constructor or copy assignment, it usually needs all three because they manage the same resource. Modern code often reaches for the Rule of Zero instead by holding a smart pointer.

interview.q: Why is `explicit` used on single-argument constructors?
interview.answer: It blocks implicit conversions from the argument type, so a function taking the class cannot silently accept a raw value. The conversion must be written at the call site.

mcq.q: In what order are members initialized?
mcq.why: The list order is ignored; members construct in the order they are declared.

mcq.q: What does a delegating constructor do?
options: Calls another constructor of the same class
mcq.answer: Calls another constructor of the same class
mcq.why: It reuses another constructor so initialization logic is not duplicated.

topics.title: Construction runs base before derived
topics.body: A derived object contains its base subobject, so the base constructor completes first and the derived body runs after. Destruction is the exact reverse: derived first, then base.

topics.title: Composition models HAS-A
topics.body: A `Car` that contains an `Engine` reuses behaviour without inheriting an interface. Composition keeps the two classes independent, which is usually the cheaper relationship to change later.

tasks.title: Forward arguments to a base constructor
tasks.statement: Write `Person(name)` and `Student(name, marks)` where `Student` passes the name to `Person`; print both fields.

debug.title: A private base member read by the derived class

interview.q: What does the diamond problem describe?
interview.answer: Two paths to the same base class create two base subobjects, so members are ambiguous and state is duplicated. Virtual inheritance collapses them into one shared base, at the cost of a more complex object layout.

interview.q: Why is composition often preferred to inheritance?
interview.answer: It couples to behaviour rather than to a type hierarchy, so the contained class can be swapped and tested independently. Inheritance is for a genuine IS-A relationship and a stable base interface.

mcq.q: Which constructor runs first for a derived object?
mcq.why: The base subobject must exist before the derived body runs.

mcq.q: A class holding another class as a member models which relationship?
mcq.why: Containment is composition, a HAS-A relationship.

topics.title: virtual makes the call wait for runtime
topics.body: A call through a base pointer to a virtual function dispatches on the dynamic type, so the derived override runs. Without virtual the call is bound statically and always picks the base version.

topics.title: A virtual destructor is not optional
topics.body: Deleting a derived object through a base pointer with a non-virtual destructor is undefined and skips the derived destructor. Making the base destructor virtual fixes the whole hierarchy.

tasks.title: Area through a base pointer
tasks.statement: Create `Shape` with a pure virtual `area()` and a `Circle(2)` override using 3.14; call it through a base pointer and print with two decimals.

debug.title: A base destructor that is not virtual
debug.error: Wrong output: base — the non-virtual base destructor skips the derived destructor.

interview.answer: Copying a derived object into a base object by value keeps only the base subobject, so the derived state and overrides are lost. Passing by reference or pointer avoids it.

interview.q: When should a function be pure virtual?
interview.answer: When the base has no sensible implementation and every concrete derived class must provide one. That turns the class into an interface that cannot be instantiated.

mcq.why: Virtual functions are resolved from the dynamic type.

options: Checks that a virtual function is actually overridden
mcq.answer: Checks that a virtual function is actually overridden
mcq.why: It turns a signature mismatch into a compile error.

topics.title: operator+ as a free function
topics.body: A free `operator+` takes both operands explicitly, so it works when the left operand is not the class type. Returning by value keeps the operands unchanged.

topics.title: operator<< returns the stream
topics.body: Returning `std::ostream&` lets `std::cout << p << " done"` chain, because each call feeds the same stream to the next. Returning void breaks every chained expression.

interview.answer: `::`, `.`, `.*`, `?:` and `sizeof`. Everything else that takes at least one class-type operand can be overloaded, though doing so should preserve the operator’s expected meaning.

interview.q: Why is `operator=` usually a member function?
interview.answer: It needs access to the object being assigned and must return `*this` by reference for chaining. The compiler-generated copy assignment is a member for the same reason.

mcq.q: What should `operator<<` for a stream return?
mcq.why: Returning the stream is what makes chained insertion work.
A free operator+ usually takes two const references.

topics.title: A function template instantiates per type
topics.body: The compiler generates a separate function for each deduced type, so `larger(3, 9)` and `larger(2.5, 1.5)` share source but not machine code. Errors appear at instantiation, not at definition.

topics.title: Non-type template parameters carry a value
topics.body: A template can take a constant value such as `int N`, which lets the size travel in the type. The array reference form below preserves the length instead of decaying to a pointer.

interview.q: Why must a template usually be defined in a header?
interview.answer: The compiler needs the definition to instantiate it for each type at the point of use. A definition hidden in a .cpp file is invisible to other translation units, producing link errors.

interview.q: What is the difference between a template and a macro?
interview.answer: A template is type-checked, scoped and instantiated by the compiler. A macro is textual substitution with no type safety, which is why templates replaced most macro-based generic code.

mcq.q: When is a function template type-checked?
mcq.why: Each instantiation is compiled for its concrete types.

mcq.q: What does `template <typename T, int N>` allow?
options: A type and a compile-time value
mcq.answer: A type and a compile-time value
mcq.why: `N` is a non-type parameter fixed at compile time.
